Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 119 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
Alberta Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 119 (South 
Irvine) is located southeast of Medicine Hat, and 
covers an area of 1,297 km2. The unit is adjacent to 
the northern border of Cypress Hills Provincial Park, 
and within Alberta’s mixedgrass natural subregion, 
with the north portion extending in to the dry 
mixedgrass natural region. Several drainages 
containing large coulee systems originate in the 
Cypress Hills and extend northward through the WMU, 
including Ross Creek, McAlpine Creek, and MacKay 
Creek. Land is primarily deeded, and general habitat 
and land use consists of cultivated cropland for the 
purpose of annual crop production, and tame and 
native grassland used for cattle grazing. Some smaller 
parcels of crown owned native grassland under 
grazing lease are also present. Oil and gas 
development is present throughout the WMU, and in 
recent years, renewable energy development has also 
increased. Chronic Wasting Disease is established 
within the WMU, with 93 positives since first detected 
in 2009 (https://open.alberta.ca/publications/chronic-
wasting-disease-in-alberta-by-wildlife-management-
unit) . Submitted samples from 2023 indicate 
prevalence rates of 34% in mule deer and 29% of 21 
mule deer bucks tested positive for the disease. 
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, 
and moose) was last conducted for WMU 119 in 2021 
using strip-transect methodology 
(https://www.alberta.ca/aerial-wildlife-survey-reports). 
The 2021 and 2025 surveys of WMU 119 with 
consistent methodology and flight dates provide an 
excellent opportunity to evaluate demographic change 
over a short time frame and supported the Alberta 
Mule Deer Collaring Project 
(https://www.apos.ab.ca/media). 
The objective of the February 2025 survey was to 
assess the status of ungulates in WMU 119 with 
estimates for abundance and age-sex composition. 
We also scanned for collared mule deer and recorded 
observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern including 
pronghorn, carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or at-
risk species. 
Survey Method 
A rotary wing (Astar-B3) transect survey was 
conducted February 8–11, 2025 flying 26 east-west 
lines at 1.6 km intervals, with 50% coverage (800 m 
wide survey strip, area surveyed 644 km2) and a total 
linear survey effort of 806 km. At each observation 
point, ungulates were classified by species, and when 
possible, sex and age were recorded. Antler size for 
deer was classified as ‘small’ (spike or two points on 
one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more 
points; antlers inside ears), or large (antlers with ≥ 4 
points, antlers outside of ears). 
Because transects varied in length, the average 
density (R) of mule deer and white-tailed deer was 
calculated by multiplying the number of animals per 
transect (∑x) by total area (km2) searched (total survey 
strip area [∑z]) (Jolly 1969, as described in Krebs 
2014). Average density (R) was multiplied by the area 
(km2) of the WMU (Z) to determine population 
estimates with 90% confidence intervals. Confidence 
interval width was calculated by multiplying the t 
statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-
distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without 
replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq 
root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-
1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number 
of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as 
the number of transects sampled. 
Elk observations were summed as a minimum total 
count (MTC) within the WMU. 
Results 
Mule Deer 
A total of 497 mule deer were observed, two collared, 
with an average groups size of 9 (range 1-54). The 
estimated density was 0.77 mule deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 1,000 individuals (90% CI 
739 – 1259). A total of 442 mule deer were 
successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio 
was estimated to be 25:100:75. That results in an 
estimated 2025 winter mule deer population of 125 
bucks, 500 does, and 375 fawns. Of the 58 mule deer

bucks classified, ten (18%) were ‘small’, 33 (59%) 
‘medium’, eight (14%) ‘large’, and six (10%) 
unclassified bucks that had dropped antlers but 
pedicels observed (older bucks tend to shed antlers 
earlier due to energy expended during rut). 
The 2025 mule deer survey results indicate a 46% 
decline in abundance from 2021. While average and 
maximum group sizes in 2025 were very similar to 
2021, with identical and high fawn:doe ratios indicating 
good recruitment, there was a marked decline in 
buck:doe ratio. Further, the proportions of antler size 
classification in mule deer shifted to younger bucks 
(14% “large” in 2025; 44% “large in 2021). While some 
of the differences between buck:doe ratios and antler 
size classification could be attributed to annual 
variation in timing of antler drop, they are consistent 
with sex and age specific CWD prevalence and 
mortality rates. Immigration patterns could also 
influence population demographics, and winter 
mortality after the 2021 survey may have also had an 
impact on mule deer abundance in WMU119.  
W
hite-tailed Deer 
A total of 649 white-tailed deer were observed with an 
average group size of 20.9 (range 1-177). The 
estimated density was 1.01/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 1305 individuals (90% CI 72 – 1858). 
A total of 228 white-tailed deer were successfully 
classified and the observed buck:doe:fawn ratio was 
4:100:73. That results in a 2025 early winter white-
tailed deer population of 29 bucks, 737 does, and 538 
fawns. 
The 2025 white-tailed deer survey results indicate a 
38% increase in abundance since 2021, an average of 
9.5%/year, well within the reproductive capacity of 
white-tailed deer. White-tailed deer exhibited a much 
higher average and maximum group size in 2025 (20.9 
vs 8, 177 vs 42, respectively), indicating a more 
clumped distribution. The extremely low buck:doe 
ratios, and observations of “unicorn” bucks, indicate 
antler drop was well-advanced by February in both 
2021 and 2025. Antlerless bucks classified as does 
would decrease both the buck and fawn:doe ratios. 
Incidental Observations 
A total of 11 moose were observed in four groups (0 
bulls, 6 cow, 5 calf). During the 2021 survey there 
were 15 moose observed. Considering this, moose 
abundance is low but stable. Three bull elk and 802 
pronghorn were observed during the survey. Other 
species observed included sharp-tailed grouse, bald 
eagle, golden eagle, porcupine, and coyote.
